Challengeth
CHAL-en-jeth
v.
From Old French chalongier (to accuse, to claim), from Latin calumniari; the archaic third-person singular form appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Exodus's law of restitution for disputed property.

Biblical Definition

Another challengeth to be his, the cause of both parties shall come before the judges.

Challengeth appears once in the Authorized Version, in Exodus's law governing disputes over lost or stolen property — ox, ass, sheep, raiment, or any manner of lost thing — when one party claims possession and another challengeth, or lays legal claim, to be his. The law's remedy is deliberately judicial rather than left to private force or accusation: the cause of both parties shall come before the judges, and whom the judges shall condemn, he shall pay double unto his neighbour (Exo 22:9). This is part of a larger body of Mosaic case law, the mishpatim of Exodus 21-23, that translates the moral demands of the Ten Commandments into concrete civil procedure for an actual nation, establishing courts, evidence, and penalties rather than leaving property disputes to whoever could assert a claim most forcefully. The doubled restitution for a false or malicious claim (as for proven theft, Exo 22:4) treats a dishonest legal challenge as itself a form of theft, punishable at the same rate, a safeguard against using the courts themselves as an instrument of injustice against an innocent neighbor. The provision reflects a consistent biblical pattern: God's law does not merely forbid theft in the abstract but builds institutions — judges, evidence, proportionate penalty — that make justice actually operable among sinful people.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from CHALLENGE: to claim as due; to demand as a right; the archaic third-person singular form here of a legal claim to disputed property, decided by judges.

CHALLENGE, v.t. To claim as due; to demand as a right; to accuse.

CHALLENGETH, v. Archaic third-person singular: he claims or accuses.

In Exodus 22:9 the word names a legal claim to disputed lost or stolen property.

The law requires judicial resolution: 'the cause of both parties shall come before the judges.'

The provision belongs to Exodus's mishpatim (21-23), translating moral law into concrete civil procedure.

Key Scripture

Exo 22:9 — "For all manner of trespass, whether it be for ox, for ass, for sheep, for raiment, or for any manner of lost thing, which another challengeth to be his, the cause of both parties shall come before the judges; and whom the judges shall condemn, he shall pay double unto his neighbour."

Modern Corruption

A modern instinct to resolve disputes informally or by whoever asserts a claim most forcefully or loudly misses the law's own insistence that property disputes be settled by established judicial process, with real accountability for a dishonest claim.

expand to see more

Where disputes are settled by social pressure, reputation, or sheer persistence rather than evidence before an appointed judge, the law's actual safeguard — accountability for a false claim, at real cost to the false claimant — is lost entirely.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Exodus's own: God cares about the mechanics of justice, not only its abstract demand, building courts and penalties that make fair resolution actually possible among sinful neighbors.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Challengeth occurs once, in Exodus's law of disputed property, requiring judicial resolution before appointed judges with doubled restitution against a dishonest claim, part of the mishpatim translating the Ten Commandments into working civil law.

Usage

"Another challengeth to be his, the cause of both parties shall come before the judges."

"Whom the judges shall condemn, he shall pay double unto his neighbour (Exo 22:9)."

"Thou shalt not steal (Exo 20:15) — the commandment this whole body of case law applies."
